syllabus.clause: relaxation in topological order in O(n + m)

at.step: Visit every vertex in topological order. At each one, relax its outgoing edges exactly once — the moment a vertex is reached, every edge into it has already been relaxed by every predecessor that could possibly improve it.

Relax the identical edges on the identical graph, but visit the vertices in some other order instead — and one vertex ends up with a distance that is simply wrong, with no error, no crash, and no warning that anything went amiss.

items.item: A topological order is not merely a convenient visiting order for this algorithm — it is the correctness proof itself, since 'every predecessor already relaxed before this vertex is visited' is exactly what a topological order guarantees and nothing else does

at.step: Visit every vertex in topological order. At each one, relax its outgoing edges exactly once — the moment a vertex is reached, every edge into it has already been relaxed by every predecessor that could possibly improve it.

items.item: This topic's single pass relaxes each edge exactly once, total work O(n + m); Dijkstra relaxes each edge at most once too but pays an extra O(log n) per relaxation for the priority queue, and Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge up to n minus one times — the acyclic precondition is what removes both the queue and the repeated rounds, not a cleverer relaxation rule

at.step: Relax the identical edges on the identical graph, but visit the vertices in some other order instead — and one vertex ends up with a distance that is simply wrong, with no error, no crash, and no warning that anything went amiss.

items.item: The wrong-order failure is silent specifically because relaxation only ever lowers a distance, never raises it back up for inspection — a vertex settled too early simply keeps whatever value it had at that moment, with no later check that would catch the mistake

at.step: Relax the identical edges on the identical graph, but visit the vertices in some other order instead — and one vertex ends up with a distance that is simply wrong, with no error, no crash, and no warning that anything went amiss.

items.item: Negating weights and re-running the identical pass works because relaxation's own comparison (less-than) is reversed consistently by negation (less-than becomes greater-than under negation, and negation's own double-reversal restores the original comparison) — it is not a coincidence specific to this one graph

items.item: Every algorithm this chapter built (Dijkstra's priority queue, Bellman-Ford's repeated rounds, Floyd-Warshall's dynamic program, Johnson's reweighting) exists specifically to handle a graph shape or weight pattern this topic's own precondition rules out by definition — this topic is not a fifth, unrelated algorithm but the limiting case where none of that machinery is needed at all

at.step: Every algorithm in this chapter answered a question between two vertices, or from one vertex to every other, on a graph that could have any shape at all. A graph with no cycle made the same question strictly easier than any of them needed to allow for.

items.item: This topic closes Chapter 18's own question (shortest and longest paths, for every kind of graph the chapter considers); the next chapter asks a different question about the same weighted graph, not about one vertex's route to the rest but about the cheapest set of edges connecting every vertex to every other

The critical path method's own attribution names 1959 only in its cited conference paper, not in the lead sentence itself, which only commits to 'the late 1950s' — a reminder that a source's own precision has a limit, and restating beyond that limit would be a claim this topic cannot actually verify
